in a read cycle and the device with that address responds in the data

Right, with access to all 16 address lines and the 8 data lines the I/O chip can select which I/O Ports it responds to internally.
Side note: all the BASICs' &()= or =&() send the entire 16 bit address Word, but the I/O chip ignores the upper Byte.

The reason for the second I/O chip is NOT for more Inputs, it is for the second AUDIO Output for STEREO!
If the two chips are interchangable there must be some external difference to force the different range of addresses.  Please send me a copy of the schematics also and I'll have a look as well.

Just my two cents, guys, but "please be nice to Adam."

He is a human being, and he has a real life, with lots of other things going on in it, and while this stuff is semi-cool ... it's also a heck of a lot of work. Since there's no financial reward in it, for him -- or anyone else! Every homebrew effort automatically equals a monetary loss, as I see it: just add up all the hours (more like or days or weeks) involved, and it's a personal loss! -- then my feeling is: let homebrew folks do things the way they feels they should be done. And be supportive of their efforts. Because, in simple pragmatic terms, if it's an attractive project TO THEM then they will want to spend time on it. And make it good. But if other people's gripes and pressure make it a chore, that will kill the fun part of it ... and, well, it shouldn't actually need explaining. Have empathy, people! Please!

But it's gonna get done on the schedule that makes sense to Adam and to me, given all of the other demands on our time and attention. Period.

Loosen up, guys. Try to think of others, as well as yourselves. The end result will be nice for you. Try to let it be nice for Adam.

Jump Table (since the routines are shifted), and the location of

CHECKSUMs #1 and 2, as well as FUDGE4 are also different, so the
un-modified BAL-CHECK should work fine on this machine as it is.

Adam - yah, it actually matches the color of the inside plastic now.  It reverses the bromine dispersal process - the actual culprit of the yellowing.  There's flame retardant in ABS plastics, and over time this can interact with oxygen to chemically break apart and the resulting breakup can disperse (literally move) the free bromine throughout the surface of the plastic, causing the yellowing and browning.  It's accelerated through exposure to ultra violet light.

The mixture used in retrobright (what the creator named it) chemically reverses the process, causing everything to bond again and therefore get rid of the yellowing.  There is no damage to the plastic in the process.

Here's the wiki set up that discusses the science, the process, and the results -

http://retr0bright.wikispaces.com/

I used the Sally's 40 vol hydrogen peroxide cream for mine, which will allow you to cut out for xantar gum, arrow root, etc.  I also did mine indoors as you can see, got a cheap 18" halogen light fixture from Wallmart (think it was around 6 bucks).  Replaced the bulb with an 18" reptile light with a high UVB.

         LD      H,(IY+CBD)      ; # v.#

         CALL DELOAD             ; # v.#
         EX   DE,HL              ; # 1 #
endif ; ##### end conditional #########

which replaced the read of HL from the Context Block DE - with the
shorter use of existing code to read in into DE and swap that into HL -
same result, two bytes shorter.

2.
Then before painting a RECTANgle with MPAINT: the HLC code flushed a 0
out through the SHIFTER

if BALLY ; ### conditional assembly ###
         XOR     A               ; fl- # extra code in ver. 0 only
         LD      (WASTE),A       ; ush #
endif ; ##### end conditional #########

more bytes.

with

if BALLY ; ### conditional assembly ###
         INC     A               ; # ! # in version 0
else ; WHITE or ASTRO ##### cond ###### else...
         ADD     A,1             ; # ? # in version 1
endif ; ##### end conditional #########

both of which set the flags up for the DAA following it, so again no
difference.

4.
Now everything after that is skewed by 5 bytes, including the
"GAME",6,"OVER",0 string used to identify the REVERSION.  One change
that was needed but didn't affect the length was in PWRUP: where they
used an UPI FILL to Clear SYSTEM RAM

         DW      $0040           ; # 0 # ... Byte Count = 64 [why ??]
else ; WHITE or ASTRO ##### cond ###### else...

         DW      $0032           ; # 1 # ... Byte Count = 50 (to $4FFF)
endif ; ##### end conditional #########

which only cleared the top line-and-a-half of the screen instead!
Also swapped the "NORMEM" and "$4000" around from the uploaded source
code (same values.)

Another byte added at CLRNUM: to CLEAR NUMBER was definitely needed to
divide the number of BCD digits by 2 to get the number of bytes with

the

bytes

Changed the comment from just "??" (meaning something to look into

At the end of the operating system was the copyright string, followed by

code which followed after that.

ICBM Attack came first. It was the experiment. And that was the only documentation I wrote for it. And we released it directly from Spectre Systems. It caught Esoterica's attention and I then wrote Treasure Cove, and Esoterica distributed it (and did the printing, etc.).

What a lot of folks may not realize is that I was finishing my EE degree at the University of Michigan, AND writing these cartridges too, and working to make money. The last two years of college was a blur (and not from drinking!!!). I was working my butt off. My main attention was on Electronics and Computers. Spectre Systems was just some fun to do with my friends. (Somehow I always ended up getting the hard work?!?)

My point, I don't remember a lot of the details, not just because I'm getting old, but because programming was just a small part of the time during that period. I was building models, blowing things up with explosives (sometimes the models), designing and building electronic projects (including a few robots), hanging out at arcades (I LOVED playing SPACE WARS http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Wars ), and watching movies (which later led to being interested in the broadcast video work I did).

So while ICBM Attack was a 'non-prototype', it was an amateur effort at marketing/sales/distribution. (Mike's job) :-)  And there were never any 'formal' instructions.

Now I'm kind of glad that I did not take a job with Astrocade. Life has turned out pretty good, so I can't complain about the path...

My latest 'project' has nothing to do with games, computers, or work...
We replaced the pool in our backyard this summer and it was a HUGE project that we are just now finishing (still have landscaping, lighting, palapa and outdoor kitchen to finish).
If you are interested, here is the website of photos tracking the project: http://web.me.com/bilbrey/Pool_Renovation/Photos.html

Brett
